headline: Family and founder-owned companies have de-rated relative to the broad market for the first time in 20 years despite sustained earnings compounding
reasoning: From 2005 to 2022 the UBS Global Family-Owned Companies Index traded at an average 30% premium to the MSCI ACWI, delivering double-digit shareholder returns against a broad market average of roughly 7% per annum. Earnings for family and founder businesses have nonetheless continued to compound at approximately 6%, implying the de-rating is driven by multiple compression rather than fundamental deterioration. Cooper Investors views this as a cyclical dislocation rather than a structural shift, and is positioning the Family and Founder Fund to benefit from a potential re-rating.

That premium has disappeared. For the first time in the two decades these companies have been tracked, the cohort today trades at a sustained discount to the broad market. The earnings, however, have kept compounding at ~6%. The willingness to pay for them has not.

headline: AI capex super-cycle mirrors internet era, with near-term winners in picks-and-shovels but durable value likely to accrue to AI-native software platforms over time
reasoning: Cooper Investors draws a parallel between the internet era and the AI age, identifying two distinct phases: a front-loaded capex super-cycle in infrastructure followed by an application-driven monetisation phase with more scalable margins. Estimates point to low-to-mid single-digit trillions in cumulative AI-heavy infrastructure spend by around 2030, favouring near-term 'picks-and-shovels' names such as chips, data centre REITs, power and thermal vendors. However, medium-term risks include a utilisation or pricing reset if demand lags the build-out. Red flags include revenue growth overly dependent on a handful of hyperscaler customers, capex intensity rising faster than gross profit, signs of overcapacity, and low margins. As with the internet age, the more durable winners are likely to be platforms and AI-native software firms that can convert sunk infrastructure into sticky workflows and high-margin recurring revenue.
quote: The AI age is replaying this with more concentrated, faster capex, centred on hyperscaler data centres, GPUs/AI accelerators, networking and power systems, with estimates pointing to low-to-mid single-digit trillions in cumulative AI-heavy infrastructure spend by around 2030. Near term, this favours 'picks‑and‑shovels' names (chips, data centre REITs, power/thermal vendors) whose top line can grow very rapidly as hyperscalers race to secure compute and energy, but whose medium‑term risk is a utilisation or pricing reset if demand lags the build‑out. As in the post-dot-com period, the more durable winners are likely to be the platforms and AI‑native software firms that can convert the sunk infra into sticky workflows and high-margin recurring revenue, rather than those whose fortunes hinge solely on the continuation of the current capex boom.

headline: Cooper Investors flags Regis Healthcare as a significant performance detractor after government funding shortfall hit earnings guidance by ~10% below consensus
reasoning: Regis Healthcare was a significant detractor from performance during the quarter after the government appeared to walk back on improved funding outcomes for the aged care sector. Under the AN-ACC model, REG will receive only a 2.6% increase in funding despite expected cost increases of 4-5%, forcing the company to update FY26 EBITDA guidance approximately 10% below consensus estimates. Cooper Investors notes this is illogical policy as it appears to favour lowest acuity residents, which would push higher-acuity patients onto the more expensive public hospital system. The funding tightening is considered a risky approach given the dire supply/demand imbalance for aged care beds, and REG has placed all greenfield and capital investment projects under review, raising concerns about future sector investment.
quote: During the quarter, a significant detractor from performance was Regis Healthcare (REG). In a "two-steps forward, one step back" process, the Government (regulators and Treasury) appear to have walked back on some of the improved funding outcomes for the sector that had become our base case following the new bi-partisan Aged Care Act. Put simply, the Government funds the Aged Care sector via two components – firstly provision of Care services and secondly for accommodation and other additional/non-care services. The Care component is funded under what is known as the AN-ACC model. REG will receive a 2.6% increase in funding based on its specific resident mix (acuity) under AN-ACC. This increase is supposed to ensure operators recover costs such as known wage increases from Fair Work, EBAs and other areas. However, a 2.6% increase is significantly less than the expected increase in REG's costs (4-5%). Near term this impacted both REG and the sector's earnings recovery. REG was forced to update the market on its estimate for FY26 EBITDA which, while ~5% higher at the midpoint of guidance vs FY25, was ~10% lower than consensus estimates. Given REG has made acquisitions, the implication is profitability in the base business is going backwards in FY26.

headline: Cooper Investors holds CME Group as a royalty-like real asset with dominant exchange network effects, high margins, and counter-cyclical revenue characteristics suited to an uncertain macro environment.
reasoning: CME is the world's largest global derivatives exchange operator, held in the portfolio since early 2024 (and previously from 2016 to 2021), sitting in the Real Assets and Income capital pool. CME generates revenue by charging per-contract fees across six diversified asset classes — interest rates, equities, FX, energy, agriculture, and metals, with crypto emerging as a seventh. The business benefits from extreme network effects ('liquidity begets liquidity'), 90%+ market share across its product sets, and group operating margins of 68%, with very high incremental margins on additional contracts. Revenues are counter-cyclical in that volatility and uncertainty drive higher trading volumes, meaning CME revenues often increase when asset prices are falling. The dominant market position has withstood multiple competitive challenges, including two attempts by Howard Lutnick (now Secretary of Commerce), both of which failed as liquidity remained decisive. CEO Terry Duy has delivered compound annual volume growth of 7%, revenue growth of 9%, EPS growth of nearly 10%, and 16% total shareholder returns over his tenure; Cooper Investors is comfortable with the depth of the executive team for succession.
quote: CME is an effective royalty on financial speculation and hedging by taking a few cents per contract traded. As trading activity expands or new types of assets are traded, revenues grow. In addition, CME is required to make minimal investment to participate in the growth of this activity. This is best demonstrated by group operating margins of 68% as each additional contract being traded on CME's exchanges delivers a very high incremental margin. In uncertain environments, volatility increases and consequently so does the need to manage risk - this drives higher trading activity and hence revenues to CME. Put another way, CME's revenues often increase when asset prices are falling. The idiosyncratic nature of CME's business means that our investment in CME provides a stabilising benefit to the broader portfolio.

headline: Cooper Investors initiated a key position in Deterra Royalties, attracted by the world-class MAC iron ore royalty following significant de-rating post Trident acquisition
reasoning: DRR was spun out of Iluka in 2020 and its primary asset is the Mining Area C (MAC) iron ore royalty, which underpins one of BHP's four large Pilbara iron ore hubs running at ~140 million dry metric tonnes per annum with a 50-year mine life disclosed by BHP. The MAC royalty is first-quartile on the cost curve and ranks among the highest quality royalties globally given its tier-1 operator and long duration. DRR significantly de-rated after acquiring UK-listed Trident Royalties and subsequently cutting its dividend payout to fund further acquisitions, creating Cooper Investors' entry opportunity. The concern is that reinvesting MAC's high-quality, fully franked cash flows into lower-returning, unfranked royalty assets risks being dilutionary and destroying value for DRR shareholders. Cooper Investors has been engaging with the Board and management to make this view clear. The fund classifies royalties under its Real Assets and Income Securities pool, viewing royalty income as higher quality than profit-based streams due to absence of operating and capex volatility.
quote: As mentioned above, our opportunity to buy DRR/MAC came after DRR acquired the UK listed Trident Royalties and the stock significantly de-rated over subsequent months... The de-rating of DRR is simple to understand. The MAC asset is a high-quality royalty and its cashflows, which had previously been streamed directly out of DRR to shareholders via fully franked dividends, are most valuable to shareholders that can fully utilise the franking credit. Investing this cashflow into risky, likely lower-returning royalty cash flows that don't have the ability to return franked dividends has a high chance of being dilutionary to MAC and destroying value for DRR shareholders. We have been engaging with the Board and management team to make our view clear.
episode_title: CI Brunswick Fund Annual Letter FY2025

However, this valuation includes just the currently producing wells and only the most economic potential wells. As discussed above, for the long-term royalty owner, long-term optionality represents material latent value. 'No value is assigned…expansions of productive trends, enhanced oil recovery, better type curves with technology, and the discovery of new pools. This…is why I own the company.' – Andrew Phillips Another way to think about this latency is as follows – using long term average energy prices we estimate PSK will earn circa 75% of its market value over the next decade in free cash flow. headline: Cooper Investors views royalty companies as structurally superior investments due to revenue-based, not profit-based, cash flows that reduce volatility and risk
reasoning: Cooper Investors classifies royalties under its Real Assets and Income Securities pool rather than treating them like conventional mining companies. A royalty is a right to receive a cashflow stream, typically a fixed percentage of revenue, which is not subject to amplification from operating or capital costs unlike profit-based streams. This makes royalty income higher quality and less risky than mining equity, and particularly attractive for long-term patient investors. The fund contrasts the quality of royalty income (MAC/DRR) with the volatility of commodity equities to justify the structural preference for the asset class.
quote: Royalty income is an attractive cash flow in contrast to a stream based on profit, which comes after operating costs and capital expenditure. What makes commodity companies more volatile or risky is the movement in revenue is amplified at the profit line after both operating costs and capital costs. As the royalty stream is not subject to fluctuations beyond revenue, it is higher quality and less risky. As an investment this makes royalties and royalty companies attractive, particularly for long-term patient investors.
episode_title: CI Brunswick Fund Annual Letter FY2025

headline: Cooper Investors initiated in Greatland Gold identifying deeply mispriced gold-copper assets in WA with a quality ex-Northern Star management team and clear catalyst to close valuation gap
reasoning: Greatland Gold is a UK-listed small cap gold producer with two key assets — Telfer and Havieron — in WA, acquired from Newmont in December 2024. Newmont was a forced seller and Greatland was the only competitive buyer given its right of first refusal, resulting in a deeply discounted acquisition price with downside protection embedded in the transaction structure. The management team, led by ex-Northern Star CFO Sean Day, has a strong track record of buying unloved assets from gold majors and improving them through entrepreneurial cost management and exploration. Since Greatland took ownership, Telfer's resource size has increased more than five times. A planned ASX secondary listing in June 2025 is expected to expand the Australian investor base and assist in closing the valuation gap relative to mid-cap ASX gold peers.
quote: Greatland's acquisition of Telfer and the remaining 70% share of Havieron from Newmont in December 2024 resonated with this attractive playbook for value creation. We were particularly drawn to the nature of the transaction - Newmont was a forced seller and Greatland was the only genuinely competitive buyer due to having a right of first refusal, leading to the acquisition being made at a deeply discounted price. Further diligence also highlighted the asymmetry of the transaction structure, including downside protection against certain operational exposures and Newmont's liabilities for further redundancies. Our investment thesis for Greatland was underscored by quality, low cost gold assets which are deeply mispriced relative to gold sector peers; value latencies in life extensions at Telfer and improved economics for the Havieron project and most critically; the right management team to drive operational excellence at the acquired assets and maximise the embedded latencies.

headline: Cooper Investors sees compelling value latency in Iluka Resources as industry supply/demand stabilises and stock trades at a fraction of book value
reasoning: Cooper Investors acknowledges being too early in its entry into Iluka Resources, noting that when investing in cyclical value situations, the firm assesses Risk-Adjusted Value Latency to be greatest when the industry is under significant pressure and the stock is priced accordingly. The firm has learned from recent experience that it is better to be slightly late than early, particularly in a market increasingly dominated by trending behaviour. However, with industry supply and demand fundamentals now stabilised and valuation at only a fraction of book value, Cooper Investors believes Risk-Adjusted Value Latency is now compelling.
quote: Another case where we have been too early to move is Iluka Resources (ILU). When investing in the Cyclical Subset of Value, we assess Risk-Adjusted Value Latency to be the greatest when the industry is under significant pressure and the stock is priced as such. In practice, signals that we are near a bottom include industry returns being at unsustainably low levels and supply/demand dynamics turning favourable as production is reduced in response to weak price signals. Reflecting on our recent experience, we have learned that it is a better to be a bit late than early. This is particularly so in a market that is increasingly dominated by trending behaviour. Notwithstanding, with industry supply and demand fundamentals, have stabilised, and valuation at only a fraction of book value, we feel that Risk-Adjusted Value Latency is compelling.

headline: Cooper Investors sees ongoing structural tailwinds for sports rights owners as legacy broadcasters and global streaming platforms intensify competition for live sport content.
reasoning: Live sport is by definition appointment viewing — it cannot be binged or churned and advertising cannot easily be avoided — making owners of unique sports assets able to monetise globally across media rights, live events, and site fees. Demand for sports media rights is rising from both traditional broadcasters and global streaming platforms including Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, and Apple, all of which view live sport as a crucial mechanism to maintain viewers and subscribers. Netflix's entry into live sports — including a landmark decade-long WWE deal — was a key inflection point, increasing competitive tension for rights. The increasingly fragmented distribution landscape means 'lock-out' risk is a material concern for media players, further strengthening the negotiating position of rights owners. CI believes sports rights remain under-monetised relative to the targeted advertising and churn-reduction benefits in a digital streaming world, despite aggregate rights values nearly doubling over the last decade.
quote: We continue to see increased demand for sports media rights from traditional broadcasters/cable as well as global streaming platforms (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon, Apple). These media companies see Live Sport as a crucial mechanism to maintain and grow viewers and/or subscribers. The increasingly fragmented distribution landscape across legacy media and streaming platforms has created a more competitive environment for sports rights. We believe a key inflection in competitiveness was Netflix's entrance into sports (on top of Amazon, Apple etc). This started with an evolution of their business model to introduce advertising supported tiers which then paved the way for the company to monetise sport assets appropriately (subscription + advertising). In fact, their first move into live sports was a landmark decade long deal with the WWE (subsequently followed by boxing, NFL deals). The work we have done suggests that sports rights in many cases remain under monetised when taking into account the targeted advertising opportunities and churn benefits which become increasingly relevant in a digital streaming world.

headline: Cooper Investors sees compelling Risk-Adjusted Value Latency in Lendlease as development returns recover and the stock trades near GFC trough valuations.

With a pathway towards reversion in development returns to more historical levels over the coming years as the cycle recovers, combined with the stock currently trading at ~0.75x last reported net tangible assets (in line with the trough of ~0.8x experienced during the GFC), we believe this opportunity represents compelling Risk-Adjusted Value Latency. Having said that, successfully executing on this long-term opportunity is likely to require a significantly greater focus and intentionality than what Lendlease has displayed historically, along with cultural change. These substantial headwinds led to very poor industry profitability and a capital strike (existing and new) in which new building approvals reached decade lows despite the strong long-term demand for new beds. We expect a marked improvement in free cashflow generation as Regis' occupancy approaches full capacity, by virtue of less room price discounting and fixed cost leverage. Assuming these were to be implemented, we estimate more than $3 per share of incremental value latency before incorporating the second order impacts of these initiatives, including the significant balance sheet optionality which would accrue, and value accretive Greenfield developments re-commencing.

headline: Cooper Investors remains bullish on Regis Healthcare, citing structural aged care reform tailwinds and >$1.50/share RAD retention optionality
reasoning: Regis reported improving occupancy (+250bps), strengthening earnings trends and growing M&A opportunity. The Aged Care Taskforce released recommendations in March 2024 that Cooper Investors views as materially more constructive for the sector than prior reviews, including potential RAD retention of up to 3% per annum (worth >$1.50/share on CI estimates) and a commitment to eliminate the ~$4/resident/day loss on daily living services. The fund argues Regis is still early in an up-cycle: industry returns need to improve further to incentivise new supply, incremental occupancy drives high incremental margins, pricing power is likely as facilities approach full capacity, and Regis's affluent resident base positions it well under any increased user-pays regime. Cash flows are expected to be strong, supporting bolt-on M&A capacity.
quote: From an investing stand-point, Regis retains attractive risk-adjusted value latency despite its recent share price outperformance. Some of the reasons we believe we are still early in the up-cycle include: industry returns still need to improve significantly to see a sustained increase in build rates; once it gets towards that level of incentive returns, there is then a long time lag between deciding to build a new facility and opening that facility (~3-4 years); in the interim, incremental occupancy is likely to drive relatively high incremental margins (despite mandated care minutes), and as facilities approach maximum occupancy there is likely to be upward pressure on room rates (pricing power); cash flows are likely to be strong reflecting their working capital position and RAD flows, which provides balance sheet capacity for value accretive bolt-on M&A; Regis is particularly well placed to benefit from increased user pays given its exposure to more affluent suburbs.

headline: Cooper Investors holds Louisiana Pacific as a low-risk turnaround driven by commodity-to-specialty transformation in siding
reasoning: Louisiana Pacific (LP) is being repositioned from a commoditised OSB manufacturer into a specialty siding business with genuine pricing power and 25-30% incremental margins. Historically, OSB was the core output of LP but is a commoditised product in which LP is a price-taker. In Atlanta we visited a construction site of homes wrapped in LP siding and met with the owner of the building company who espoused the virtues of the product. headline: Cooper Investors highlights LSEG's intentional and ahead-of-schedule clearance of the Refinitiv acquisition overhang as a key positive catalyst
reasoning: Following the transformative Refinitiv acquisition (first announced in 2019), LSEG faced a significant equity overhang as the selling consortium (Blackstone and Thomson Reuters) held ~36% of LSEG shares, with three tranches of ~12% scheduled to be sold from January 2023, 2024, and 2025 onward. Such overhangs typically weigh on a stock's performance for years. The board demonstrated 'Intentionality' in resolving this ahead of schedule through accelerated direct buybacks funded by strong operating cash flow, coordinated open market placings during periods of strong markets, and a direct purchase by Microsoft of a 4% stake from the seller. The overhang is now close to gone approximately 18 months ahead of schedule, while LSEG simultaneously reduced balance sheet debt and over-achieved on revenue growth targets.
quote: After the acquisition of Refinitiv (first announced in 2019) LSEG had a long execution to-do list in addition to managing a change in capital structure. Given the transformative size of the Refinitiv deal, LSEG could not pay entirely in cash and had to issue new equity as part of the consideration. This meant the selling consortium (consisting largely of Blackstone and Thomson Reuters) became the largest investor in LSEG, owning ~36% at deal completion. A managed exit was structured such that, after a 2-year lock-up, three tranches of ~12% could be sold from January 2023, 2024, and 2025 onward. The consortium also controlled several board seats which would reduce in number as pre-agreed ownership thresholds were crossed on the way to zero. In market parlance, this situation represents an 'overhang', something markets dislike with investors wary of entering a stock story knowing a material amount of equity is due in future. This kind of overhang can linger over a stock for many years and drag on performance. Here we have been impressed with the board's recognition of the impact on potential value creation and their Intentionality in getting it cleaned up as quickly as possible... after a recent additional placing the overhang is now close to gone almost 18 months ahead of schedule. This is an excellent outcome, especially while simultaneously reducing balance sheet debt and over-achieving on revenue growth targets.

headline: Cooper Investors initiates position in Union Pacific as new CEO Jim Vena's return signals an operational excellence inflection that should unlock significant financial performance improvement
reasoning: UNP is described as a Stalwart investment made earlier this year and is characterised as a privileged business within a wonderful industry, structurally, geographically, and financially. Despite its natural advantages, UNP has lagged rail peers in service and growth for over a decade following the departure of its COO Jim Vena in 2021. UNP is North America's largest publicly listed railroad, both in revenue and route miles. Its network spans more than 32,500 route miles (52,000kms), serving the Western two thirds of the US... Enter Jim Vena, a lifelong railroader with more than forty years of experience beginning his career in 1976 as a Canadian National labourer, working his way to Conductor, Engineer, Trainmaster, up to Chief Operating Officer under legendary railroader E Hunter Harrison. Following his departure, service metrics lagged peers, flowing onto mediocre financial performance and recent years have seen investors and activists push hard for change at the top. In August Jim triumphantly returned as CEO to lead Union Pacific into a new era of operational excellence, injecting the Intentionality and Focused Management Behaviour that has been lacking. headline: Cooper Investors sees a highly attractive demand/supply dynamic in Australian aged care over the medium term, driven by a capital strike, supply attrition, and accelerating 85+ population growth through FY32.

headline: Cooper Investors initiated a position in Aurizon after a 15%-plus share price drop, citing trough earnings, infrastructure-like asset undervaluation, and multiple growth catalysts

Cooper Investors identifies FY23 as the trough earnings year, with growth catalysts including volume recovery, India-driven met coal demand, CPI-linked contracts above cost inflation, efficiency savings via outsourcing and 'trainguard' technology, a significant WACC reset for regulated track revenue, and new bulk contract wins. US railroad peers have achieved 15-20% EPS growth p.a. from just 1-2% volume growth via pricing and mix benefits, and Aurizon's management team and board are rated highly by the firm. At that point Aurizon was trading on a 12-13x PE ratio. At a headline level, this is a low rating given Aurizon is an infrastructure-like business... If we were to apply this 1.3x multiple to Aurizon, then the market is ascribing very little value to the rest of Aurizon's business. Regardless of how we value the stock, Aurizon appears 'cheap' relative to comparable infrastructure assets and offshore listed railroad peers. On closer inspection post its half year result, it was clear to us that FY23 will be the trough year for earnings for Aurizon and there are a number of reasons why earnings should grow solidly in coming years.

headline: Cooper Investors views Aurizon as offering near-term earnings growth from regulated returns and normalising coal volumes, with bulk providing a longer-term hedge as energy transition proceeds
reasoning: Coal represents 86% of Aurizon's 1H23 earnings and offers material near-term growth: the regulated return building blocks for FY24-27 are largely known, and coal haulage volumes have been suppressed by above-average rainfall over three years and are expected to recover with the onset of an El Niño event. Longer term, coal will be a headwind but Australian coal is expected to gain market share given its higher quality and lower production cost. Investment in bulk provides partial mitigation, as bulk contracts are above the cost of capital and trains can be repurposed. quote: Coal was 86% of Aurizon's earnings in 1H23 and offers material near-term growth given: i) the building blocks for the regulated return on the below rail business for the period FY24-27 are largely known; and ii) coal haulage volumes have been impacted by above average rainfall over the past three years, which is expected to improve with the commencement of an El Niño event (as predicted by the Bureau of Meteorology). Coal will be a headwind in the medium to long-term as the world transitions to clean energy, but Australian coal is expected to take market share given it is higher quality (less emissions) with a lower cost-to-produce. Aurizon's investment in bulk should also partly mitigate the impact. Bulk contract returns are expected to be lower than thermal or met coal contracts but are still above the company's cost of capital (particularly where trains can be repurposed). We also see bulk as a partial hedge for coal as the energy transition proceeds given the quantum of critical minerals that will be required to meet global net zero objectives.

quote: EBOS (EBO) underperformed on news they were unsuccessful in renewing their Chemist Warehouse pharmaceutical supply contract, which was instead awarded to Sigma (SIG). EBOS currently generates ~$1.9bn of revenue from the Chemist Warehouse contract annually, which will expire June 2024. In our view, the share price reaction was proportional to the earnings lost from the contract renegotiations. The renewal of the Chemist Warehouse contract was never guaranteed. EBOS performed its obligations under the contract to a high standard. However, this was overshadowed by Sigma's offer that included issuing Chemist Warehouse with shares equal to 10.7% of SIG issued share capital. The board and management of EBOS have always acknowledged the risk that contract renewal presented and developed strategies to minimise the earnings impact of this outcome. reasoning: BKNG is the world's largest online travel agent operating the Booking.com brand and plays a critical aggregator role in fragmented travel accommodation. The company is expanding its 'Connected Trip' strategy to link all components of travel including flights, car hire, and entertainment, which should improve consumer experience and generate additional revenue streams. quote: BKNG is the world's largest online travel agent, known for its key brand Booking.com. It is an exceptional business. BKNG plays the valuable role of aggregator in a fragmented travel market, particularly in travel accommodation. Customers tend to travel infrequently and often to new places hence the importance of BKNG's wide selection and extensive consumer reviews. Accommodation providers on the other hand have high fixed costs but low variable ones, offering room nights that are perishable in nature. As a result they highly value BKNG's demand generation capabilities. BKNG today is expanding its role in the travel ecosystem, moving from mainly accommodation bookings to all key components of a trip, including flights, car hire and entertainment. This 'Connected Trip' strategy should improve the consumer travel experience by linking up previously fragmented components. It should also create additional sources of revenue for BKNG and increase overall business quality as more consumers interact with the Booking.com app. BKNG is run for the long term by CEO Glenn Fogel, a 20-year veteran of the group. We see Value Latency arising from the COVID impact on travel coupled with historic investor concern on competitive intensity, which has fallen. BKNG today trades on a Free Cash Flow multiple of ~15x for an industry leader with exceptional financial quality. It is well capitalised for growth and the bulk of cash generation comes back to owners via share buybacks – last year BKNG repurchased almost 8% of its share count. We expect this to continue, with an ongoing recovery in travel delivering double digit earnings per share growth.

headline: Cooper Investors highlights systemic fragility of fractional reserve banking and inadequacy of post-GFC liquidity standards following SVB and Credit Suisse collapses
reasoning: The collapses of SVB and Credit Suisse illustrate that the post-GFC LCR liquidity standards proved inadequate in practice, as they underestimate the potential for sustained outflows beyond 30 days, correlated outflows across the system and the speed of outflows in a digital world. SVB operated a risky asset-liability mismatch that investors appear to have missed or willingly ignored, while Credit Suisse's LCR was well above the regulatory minimum yet still succumbed to a liquidity crisis. The firm draws the lesson that each crisis is subtly different and that trying to predict the next Black Swan is futile; instead, the firm seeks anti-fragile companies that are robust against such shocks or have a sufficiently large margin of safety.
quote: While there were company-specific risk management shortcomings that contributed to both unravelling, as is often the case in a banking crisis, it was liquidity concerns brought them undone. Ironically, at 144%, Credit Suisse most recent quarterly Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) was well above the regulatory minimum. Incredibly, it was close to 200% in the prior quarter (3Q22). Despite their good intent and apparent sophistication, the post-GFC liquidity standards proved inadequate. The LCR framework appears to underestimate the potential for sustained outflows for longer than 30 days, correlated outflows across the system and the speed with which outflows can occur in a digital world.

headline: Cooper Investors cautious on Australian major banks as funding costs rise and multiple headwinds compound, but remains open-minded to value emerging
reasoning: While Australia's major banks are among the strongest and most tightly regulated in the world and Cooper Investors harbours no serious systemic concerns, the banks are not immune to global fallout from the SVB and Credit Suisse episodes. Funding costs are likely to rise, compounding existing pressures from intense mortgage competition, rising deposit betas, falling credit growth, cost inflation and potential asset quality deterioration. The prospect of regulatory relief (e.g. softening of APRA's IRRBB capital requirement) now appears unlikely; indeed, regulators may apply closer scrutiny to liquidity stress scenario methodologies, and holding more and higher quality liquidity would grind further on industry returns. Cooper Investors nonetheless remains open-minded to the possibility that further underperformance could eventually make risk-adjusted value latency look more attractive for the banks.
quote: Australia's major banks are among the strongest and most tightly regulated in the world; hence, we do not harbour any serious systemic concerns here. However, this does not make them immune to the global fallout. Funding costs are likely to rise, which compounds the existing pressure forming from intense mortgage competition, rising deposit betas, falling credit growth, cost inflation and the spectre of asset quality deterioration as cost-of-living pressures rise. We also suspect that any potential regulatory relief, such as a softening of APRA's unique Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB) capital requirement, is now unlikely too. Indeed, it seems more likely that regulators will give closer scrutiny to the methodologies involved in calculating liquidity stress scenarios. Holding more and higher quality liquidity would grind down further on industry returns. However, in the spirit of Mark Twain's quote above, we remain open-minded to the possibility that further underperformance could eventually make risk-adjusted value latency look more attractive for the banks.

headline: Cooper Investors increasingly constructive on semiconductors, citing supply-side rationalisation, structural demand growth and geostrategic onshoring tailwinds

On the demand side there is seemingly insatiable appetite for both leading edge and mature nodes driven by new use cases as technology penetrates further into modern society.

As commodity prices stagnate at elevated levels, or even begin to retrace back to more reasonable prices, we will, and are beginning to see, margin pressure in mining companies.

headline: Cooper Investors views Rentokil's acquisition of Terminix positively, citing route density economics, brand value, and Rentokil's strong integration track record as key drivers of value creation.
reasoning: Rentokil announced an intention to acquire Terminix Global Holdings for approximately US$6bn, which will roughly double its Pest Control business in North America and make it the number one player in the US market. Cooper Investors highlights three reasons for confidence: (1) route density economics, where adding Terminix's ~375 branches to Rentokil's network creates significant branch and route synergies with up to 5-10 margin points of uplift in a single region; (2) the Terminix brand, which is the most recognised pest control brand in the US with strong consumer sentiment and lower customer acquisition costs; and (3) pattern recognition, as Terminix has been a neglected subsidiary of a former conglomerate whose underperformance relative to potential should unwind under Rentokil's ownership. The firm views the ~14x EV/EBITDA post-synergies price as reasonable for a mid-single digit growth annuity service business elevated to market leadership in the world's best pest control market.
quote: While we are typically wary of large acquisitions that attract the label of 'transformational' we feel positive about this transaction for several reasons. Firstly, route density economics... In acquiring the ~375 branches of Terminix in one fell swoop, Rentokil has a big opportunity to extract branch and route synergies. Secondly, the brand. Rentokil is not just acquiring an estate of branches and technicians, but in Terminix is getting the most recognised brand in Pest Control in the US that's been around for a hundred years... This brand has tremendous awareness and value which Rentokil don't appear to be paying much if anything for. Thirdly, pattern recognition. The last decade at Terminix has seen constant change of ownership, corporate structure, philosophy and turnover at executive management level... We have seen this movie play out before – a high quality acquirer with a strong integration team has an opportunity to clear out obstacles and problems that have been holding back performance and allow the full potential of what is still a fundamentally good business to flourish. Paying around 14x EV/EBITDA post synergies seems like a reasonable price to pay for a mid-single digit growth annuity service business that elevates them to number one in the US, the world's best Pest Control market.

headline: Cooper Investors expects CSL's FY22 to be weak due to plasma collection disruption from COVID but anticipates earnings growth recovery thereafter
reasoning: CSL's share price fell approximately 20% from its highs before partially recovering, driven primarily by disruption to plasma collections — the key raw material input for its core IVIG product. COVID restricted movement and made plasma donors nervous about attending collection centres, causing a sharp drop in collections. Although collections are now recovering in the US (CSL's main collection market), the nine-month lag between collection and final product sale means the volume impact will be felt in FY22 results. Additional cost headwinds include higher payments to attract donors and extra centre preparation costs. The one offsetting factor is that IVIG prices have risen in both the US and Europe. Cooper Investors expects FY22 to produce a weak result but for growth to pick up again beyond the current financial year.
quote: CSL has had a bumpy ride over the last twelve months – falling by 20% from its share price highs and then partially recovering the drop. The main issue the company has been facing is collections of plasma, the raw material input into making its core product IVIG which is used to both improve and save lives. The onset of Covid has both restricted movement generally and made plasma donees nervous about attending plasma centres to donate. Collections dropped somewhat precipitously last year and although collections are now recovering in the USA (CSL's main market for collections), the nine month lag between plasma collection and final product sale means the impact will only be seen in the upcoming financial year profits. In addition to weakness in the volume of collections, CSL has had to pay more for its collections, as well as incur extra cost to equip its collection centres, to encourage donees into the centres. The one offsetting factor has been that prices for IVIG have risen in both the USA and Europe. We expect FY22 to produce a weak result but for growth to pick up again beyond the current financial year.

Cooper Investors views most of these issues as transitory rather than structural, noting Indonesia and Peru are already recovering, NSW thermal coal exports have found markets outside China, and the SAP system is operational though not yet optimal. A new CEO, Sanjeev Gandhi, with 26 years at BASF is viewed positively. While an additional earnings rebasing at the interim result is possible, CI sees this as the cyclical bottom. The combination of self-help initiatives and Orica's technology investments to transform drill and blast operations and improve mine process productivity underpin the investment thesis.
quote: We believe most of these issues to be transitory, rather than structural, in nature. Indonesia and Peru are already back or on the way back to normal. In recent months NSW thermal coal exports are back to slightly above last year, even with China still refusing to allow the importation of Australian coal, having found an end-market outside of China. The impact of the pandemic will reduce as the world moves forward with the rollout of the vaccine and/or mine processes adjust to deal with the pandemic risks... Despite all the challenges, Orica continues to improve the business through investment, rationalising operations and implementation of the new enterprise planning software. This will put the business in a position, post-pandemic, to take full advantage of improving end-markets. This opportunity for self-help, combined with the company's investment in technology that has the potential to transform the drill and blast operations of mining companies and improve end-to-end mine process productivity, underpin our investment proposition for Orica.
episode_title: CI Australian Equities Fund Quarterly Report 31 March 2021

headline: Cooper Investors initiated a position in Orica during Q1 2021 following a material profit downgrade, viewing the earnings loss as temporary and ORI as a later-cycle beneficiary of rising commodity prices
reasoning: The fund purchased ORI shares at a low price relative to asset value following a material profit downgrade and stock de-rating, drawing comparison to its BHP purchase during the Covid lows. Earnings pressure over the past 12 months stemmed from pandemic impacts on customers in South/Central America, Europe, and Africa, compounding disruptions in Indonesia, Peru, and Australia related to weather, social unrest, and Chinese coal bans, as well as costs from a troubled SAP implementation. The fund believes most of these issues are transitory, with Indonesia and Peru already recovering, NSW thermal coal exports back above prior year levels, and pandemic effects set to ease. Elevated commodity prices are seen as a leading indicator for stronger mining activity, which will benefit ORI as a drill and blast products and services provider. The appointment of new CEO Sanjeev Gandhi is viewed as a positive development, and ORI's ongoing investment in technology to transform drill and blast operations underpins the investment proposition.
quote: During the quarter the Fund initiated a position in Orica (ORI) following a material profit downgrade and stock de-rating. In short our view is this loss of earnings is temporary, and that ORI is in fact likely to be a later cycle beneficiary of the current strength in commodity prices (which are a leading indicator for stronger mining activity). Our purchase of the shares was at a low price relative to ORI's asset value, in a manner similar to our purchase of BHP during the height of the pandemic. ORI's earnings have been under pressure over the last 12 months due to the effects of the pandemic on ORI's customers, particularly in South/Central America, Europe and Africa. This resulted in lower levels of production at mines and thus lower demand for drill & blast products and services. We expect a significant improvement in performance as the pandemic abates and mining operations get back to normal. The heightened level of commodity prices is evidence of the improved demand environment and supports a strong return to mining activity.
episode_title: CI Brunswick Fund Quarterly Report 31 March 2021

headline: Cooper Investors flags rising labour costs and supply constraints in Western Australia's mining sector as elevated commodity prices and closed borders drive shortages, with mid-tier miners eyeing previously shelved projects.
reasoning: Following visits to Perth, CI observed that Western Australia has been relatively unscathed by COVID, with elevated commodity prices — particularly iron ore — providing a significant economic boost. However, consistent industry feedback indicated that labour shortages are emerging due to high levels of activity and closed state borders, which is beginning to impact capital project costs in mining and housing construction. CI expects these labour cost pressures to creep into operating costs for miners. Additionally, high iron ore prices are incentivising mid-tier miners to revisit previously shelved volume projects.
quote: We headed over to Perth for the first time in about 18 months and met with mining contacts across a range of commodities including iron ore, gold, copper, lithium, mineral sands and rare earths. It's clear that the state has been relatively unscathed by COVID as the elevated commodity prices, in particular iron ore, have been a massive boon for the economy... The consistent feedback was that, given the increasing level of work across the state and because the borders have been shut, labour shortages are beginning to assert themselves. This is impacting the costs of capital projects across the mining sector, and housing related construction costs. It is expected that this will creep into the operating costs for the miners, if it has not done so already. The high iron ore price is also incentivising the mid-tier miners to consider bringing on additional volume from previously shelved projects.
episode_title: CI Australian Equities Fund Quarterly Report 31 March 2021

headline: Cooper Investors argues fuel retailing industry structure supports profitability of leading operators for many years despite long-term EV transition risk
reasoning: The fund acknowledges that concerns about ALD and ZEL operating in sunset industries are a long-dated risk, but argues several structural factors support industry profitability for many years. Barriers to exit are low given housing redevelopment optionality, but micro-economics at the site level mean profitability depends on margin as well as volume. A large proportion of sub-scale sites means volume is likely to migrate to stronger sites, driving higher incremental margins. ICE vehicles have average asset ages of ~20 years and new car purchases represent only ~5% of existing stock, implying a long sunset period. Political palatability of taxes on ICE vehicles is seen as low, further delaying transition headwinds.
quote: While this is no doubt a long-dated risk, there are a number of reasons why we believe the structure of the industry and the profitability of leading operators is likely to remain supportive for many years to come: The barriers to exit in the service station industry are quite low particularly with housing a 'higher and better use' option in many locations. The economics of the industry are driven by the micro-economics at a site level where profitability is a function of not just volume but also margin. A large proportion of the industry retail sites are sub-scale. For instance, in NZ 15% of the industry is sub 2.5ML per annum. In effect, much of this volume is likely to migrate to stronger sites driving higher incremental margins as the fixed costs of the stronger sites won't change materially. Internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles currently have asset ages of ~20 years and the number of brand new cars purchased relative to existing stock is only 5% which likely drives a long sunset period for the industry.
episode_title: CI Brunswick Fund Quarterly Report 31 March 2021

headline: Cooper Investors remains invested in Oz Minerals but flags elevated speculative activity in copper as a key near-term risk
reasoning: Oz Minerals had a strong year of outperformance in 2020, completing the Carrapateena mine ramp-up 6 months ahead of schedule, acquiring Cassini, and advancing studies on Prominent Hill, West Musgrave, and other projects. Management under Andrew Cole has substantially transformed the business since 2014, and Cooper Investors sees further value creation potential across the project pipeline. However, the copper price at above US$3.50/lb appears at the top end of the cost curve in a broadly balanced market, and cheap money and excess liquidity appear to be driving speculative activity. While long-term electrification trends support copper demand, the firm notes speculative bubbles in green-linked commodities have a tendency to come and go.
quote: Currently, our key concern with OZ Minerals as an investment proposition is the elevated level of speculative activity evident in the copper market. The copper price currently sits above US$3.50/lbs. This is at the top end of the cost curve in a market that appears to be broadly balanced in terms of supply and demand. We do see the need for elevated prices over time to incentivise additional supply, particularly if the electrification of the economy becomes the primary solution to deliver a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. However, as we have seen in other 'green' linked commodities, speculative bubbles have a tendency to come and go, driven by periods of excess of supply or demand, even as the longer term trends continue to play out. It would appear as if the cheap money and excess liquidity, mentioned in the introduction above, is not just flowing into equities markets. Irrespective of shorter term fluctuations in the copper price, we are confident that OZL's management team will continue to execute on the opportunities they have with a clear intent of creating value for shareholders, as has been evidenced over the past year.

quote: For all WDAY's success and averaging over 35% p.a. sales growth the share has barely outperformed the S&P500 since early 2014 as its sales multiple declined from 26x to 10x. WDAY now trades on a more reasonable but still elevated FCF multiple of 43x. However on our view of normalised margins this multiple of FCF would be even lower, below 30x. WDAY is investing to grow its top line 20-25% and if they were to slowdown and grow in line with the market (around 10%) we would expect to see a typical 30%+ software margin, up from the 17% reported margin today. headline: Cooper Investors Brunswick Fund focuses on proprietorial management styles including family-linked, founder-led and owner-operator companies with strong governance qualities
reasoning: The fund's investment universe is organised around three broad categories: family-linked and founder-led companies, owner-operator cultures, and specialised focused managers resetting governance and management priorities. These proprietorial management styles are characterised by behavioural qualities including focus, humility, alignment with shareholder interests, deep industry knowledge, value and risk-based capital allocation (often counter-cyclical), and investment in skills, talent and innovation. The manager views these attributes as key drivers of long-term value creation and portfolio outperformance.
quote: 3 broad categories: 1. Family-linked and founder-led companies. 2. Owner-operator cultures. 3. Specialised, focused managers who are resetting governance and management priorities. All of these proprietorial management styles have the following behavioural qualities: • Focus – intentional and know what they are doing. • Humility – authentic, energetic and focussed on long-term value. • Alignment with and respect for shareholder interests. • Deep, nuanced knowledge of the business/industry. • Value and risk-based capital allocation (often counter-cyclical). • Invest in skills, talent and innovation.

headline: Cooper Investors sees Eureka Group as the emerging scaled player in fragmented affordable seniors rental market with strong incremental returns
reasoning: Eureka Group delivered a resilient FY20 result despite Covid-19, growing occupancy by 400bps, EPS by 19%, NTA by 6%, and maintaining stable gearing. The company benefits from quasi-government backing, demographic tailwinds, free cash flow generation, and a property/land-backed asset base. Incremental returns from acquiring additional villages exceed 20%, reflecting attractive acquisition pricing and EGH's sub-scale nature where corporate overheads exceed 60% of PBT. A corporate governance reset 18 months ago is now bearing fruit, and the addition of Greg Paramor AO to the board is viewed as a key positive given his track record of scaling property businesses.
quote: Despite Covid-19, the company increased occupancy 400bps, grew EPS 19%, achieved 6% growth in net tangible assets and maintained stable gearing levels. We continue to see a significant opportunity for Eureka Group to become the scaled player in this highly fragmented market. Importantly, incremental returns from acquiring additional villages are high (>20%) reflecting attractive acquisition pricing (15%+ levered IRR's) combined with EGH's sub-scale nature (corporate overheads >60% of PBT). Given this opportunity, we think the addition of Greg Paramor AO to the EGH Board is a key positive.

headline: Cooper Investors shifts portfolio from underweight to modestly overweight Cyclicals after pandemic-driven price dislocations
reasoning: Over the last 12 months the portfolio has moved from being underweight Cyclicals to being modestly overweight. The pandemic-driven underperformance created buying opportunities in several cyclical names. The key shared characteristic across the additions is the combination of management capability and opportunity to add substantial value over the next few years.
quote: Over the last 12 months the portfolio has moved from being underweight Cyclicals, to being modestly overweight as at the end of the quarter. Cyclical stocks added to the portfolio this year include Lend Lease (LLC) and Santos (STO), while the portfolio has also increased holdings in BlueScope Steel (BSL), Orica (ORI) and Oz Minerals (OZL). All of these companies had experienced some underperformance during the pandemic outbreak, which provided us with an opportunity to buy the stocks at better prices. However, the key characteristic that they all have in common is the combination of opportunity and management capability to add substantial value over the course of the next few years.

headline: Cooper Investors remains cautious on Australian banking sector despite emerging value, citing limited ability to grow earnings in a difficult operating environment
reasoning: Despite some value latency becoming evident in the banking sector, Cooper Investors remains cautious because banks have limited opportunity to add value in the current environment. Low interest rates are compressing margins, loan growth is subdued, bad debt resolution remains unclear, and ongoing regulatory pressures persist. The firm believes other industries offer better prospects for value creation over its 2–3 year investment horizon.
quote: This is one of the primary reasons why we remain cautious on the banking sector, despite some value latency becoming evident. The sector as a whole has limited opportunity to add value, particularly in the context of a difficult operating environment. With low interest rates compressing margins, subdued loan growth, unclear bad debt resolution and ongoing regulatory pressures, we are finding companies in other industries with better prospects for value creation over the time frame that we look to invest.
